## Abstract

Understanding how food web structure varies across broad spatial gradients is essential for identifying general principles of ecosystem organization and resilience under global change. We analyzed seven highly resolved marine food webs spanning a latitudinal gradient from 48°S to 78°S in the Southwest Atlantic and Antarctic region to evaluate how ecosystem size, latitude, human impact, and number of species shape network structure and dynamic stability. We quantified multiple topological and dynamical properties, including connectance, link density, mean trophic level, modularity, dynamic stability (maximum eigenvalue), SVD-based complexity, and rank deficiency. We then modeled their relationships with environmental predictors using site-level Bayesian regressions that incorporate the uncertainty derived from a metaweb assembly model as a measurement-error term. Because our dataset comprises only seven independent food webs, we additionally assessed the robustness of every detected relationship using a leave-one-site-out procedure. We considered an effect robust only if it was not driven by the inclusion of any single food web.

Ecosystem area was the only predictor whose effects met this robustness criterion: larger ecosystems supported higher trophic levels, greater interaction density, and higher structural complexity (SVD complexity), and these associations persisted when individual food webs were excluded from the analysis. Positive effects of latitude on connectance, link density, trophic level and complexity, and effects of the number of trophic species on modularity, rank deficiency and connectance, were also detected under the full dataset but did not consistently survive site-exclusion, indicating sensitivity to the particular composition of this dataset rather than general patterns. Human impact effects were weak and uncertain throughout, likely because the cumulative impact index integrates multiple stressors whose effects on food web structure may differ in magnitude and direction.

These results indicate that, among the environmental gradients considered, ecosystem area is the most defensible driver of marine food web structure and resilience in the Southwest Atlantic, while latitudinal and number of species patterns detected here should be treated as exploratory hypotheses pending confirmation with additional independent food webs.

## Introduction

Understanding how ecological network structure varies across broad spatial gradients can reveal general principles of ecosystem organization and how anthropogenic drivers shape ecosystem functioning. In marine systems, food webs integrate multiple ecological processes and functions such as energy transfer, species interactions, and functional organization that collectively determine ecosystem resilience and stability under environmental change. As a result, trophic interaction networks provide a powerful framework for evaluating ecosystem responses to both natural gradients and human‐induced stressors.

Marine food webs across the Southern Hemisphere are exposed to distinct yet often overlapping stressors, including fishing pressure, ocean warming, biological invasions, sea ice decline, and glacial retreat, each expected to leave characteristic signatures on food web structure and stability [@Queiros2024]. A recent review spanning the Southwest Atlantic and Antarctic regions compiled evidence linking dominant regional stressors to potential changes in food-web connectance, modularity, stability, energy fluxes, and functional diversity [@Marina2024b]. The review suggested that food-web responses may be strongly context dependent, with local processes operating across broad spatial gradients potentially mediating how stressors translate into network reorganization.

To evaluate how environmental and spatial factors influence the structure and stability of marine trophic networks, we adopt a macroecological approach to explicitly test these hypotheses by analysing a suite of complexity, structure,  and stability metrics in relation to broad environmental gradients, including latitude, area, human impact, depth, and the number of trophic species. This approach aligns with ongoing efforts [@Frelat2022;@Jordan2024] to identify general mechanisms governing ecological network organization across spatial scales and environmental contexts [@Welti2015; @Cirtwill2015].

According to the ecosystem size hypothesis, larger ecosystems are expected to sustain longer food chains due to higher species richness, greater habitat heterogeneity, and increased persistence of higher trophic levels [@Post2000; @Post2007]. Empirical support for this pattern has been reported for both freshwater and marine systems [@Takimoto2008]. However, food chain length is not determined by ecosystem size alone. Community organization and energetic constraints can impose upper limits on trophic structure, particularly when large-bodied taxa feed at relatively low trophic positions. In such cases, energy pathways to top predators may saturate at lower trophic levels, resulting in shorter mean food chain lengths despite high productivity or large ecosystem size [@Post2002]. This mechanism predicts that food webs dominated by large herbivorous or omnivorous consumers will exhibit systematically shorter food chains than webs lacking such taxa [@Arim2016; @Jardine2016]. Consistent with this view, studies of marine food webs have found no universal latitudinal pattern in food chain length or maximum trophic level, suggesting that biogeographic gradients interact with community composition and energetic constraints rather than acting as simple drivers [@JakeVanderZanden2007].

Another key dimension shaping food web structure is human-driven impact [@Kraufvelin2026]. Anthropogenic pressures are often hypothesized to erode network organization and drive food webs toward more random structures, potentially reducing ecological complexity and stability [@Mestre2022]. However, empirical patterns depend strongly on ecosystem type. At a global scale, regions with higher disturbance tend to exhibit more random network structures, whereas less disturbed systems show a greater prevalence of scale-free organization. Notably, marine food webs appear to deviate from this general pattern, exhibiting a shift toward more scale-free structures with increasing human impact [@Mestre2022]. Empirical evidence from marine systems therefore remains mixed, with reported changes in connectance and energy pathways varying across ecosystems and spatial contexts [@Mestre2022]. In parallel, recent global syntheses indicate that connectance in marine food webs tends to increase toward higher latitudes, although this pattern is partly confounded by variation in species richness and by differences between coastal and oceanic systems [@Albouy2019].

Network modularity represents another important structural property linking food web organization to stability. Modular structures are assumed to buffer ecosystems against perturbations by constraining the spread of disturbances across the network [@Thebault2010]. Because environmental gradients and anthropogenic pressures act as sources of external perturbations, ecological networks are expected to exhibit structural configurations that promote stability under such conditions [@Monteiro2017; @Borrelli2015]. Consequently, modularity may vary systematically along environmental gradients or in response to climate change and human activities, reflecting emergent adaptive responses of local food web organization to disturbance regimes.

Taken together, these frameworks suggest that ecosystem size, latitude, depth, and human disturbance may each contribute, independently or through interacting pathways that a dataset of seven food webs cannot fully disentangle, to the organization, stability, and functional complexity of marine trophic networks. By evaluating these predictors individually across a broad latitudinal gradient in the Southwest Atlantic - Antarctic region, and by explicitly testing the robustness of each detected relationship to the exclusion of individual food webs, our study provides a conservative assessment of which large-scale environmental gradients most defensibly structure marine food webs under contrasting ecological and anthropogenic contexts.

## Methods

### Food web data and standardization

All the food webs considered in the present study have been previously described in individual peer-reviewed publications [San Jorge Gulf in @Funes2022; Beagle Channel in @Rodriguez2022; Burdwood Bank in @Marina2024a; North and South Scotia Sea in @Lopez-Lopez2022; Potter Cove in @Marina2018; Weddell Sea in @Jacob2011]; for a comprehensive overview see also [@Marina2024b]. The food webs span a latitudinal gradient from the San Jorge Gulf (48°S) to the Weddell Sea (78°S), covering a range of ecosystem types, including coastal bays, continental shelf areas, and open-ocean systems (Figure 1). 
Although these food webs were constructed using a similar methodology [@Gauzens2013], we identified dissimilarities in the trophic resolution of several functional groups (e.g., phytoplankton, zooplankton, marine mammals, and seabirds). To minimise this trophic disparity among datasets, we modified the food webs in the following way:
For the Beagle Channel, North and South Scotia Sea, we increased the resolution of high-trophic levels, that is, we added marine mammals and seabirds as well as their diets.
For the North and South Scotia Sea and the Weddell Sea, we reduced the resolution of basal species mainly by collapsing the community diversity of phytoplankton into functional groups (e.g., Bacillariophyceae, Chrysophyceae, Dinophyceae). By applying the same criteria to all food webs, these adjustments harmonized the overall trophic structure across networks while preserving their key ecological structure, enabling robust cross-site comparisons along the latitudinal gradient. With this, we aim to tackle issues with food web resolution when comparing food web structures compiled by different researchers [@Brimacombe2025]. Details on the standardization process are available in the Supplementary Material.

### Human Impact Index

To quantify anthropogenic pressure on marine ecosystems, including climate-driven stressors, we used the most recent version of the cumulative human impact index developed by @Halpern2025, which has been widely applied in marine ecological and network-based studies [@Mestre2022; @Foley2015]. This index integrates spatially explicit data on multiple human pressures acting on marine ecosystems, combining both current conditions and projected impacts.

The updated framework incorporates ten anthropogenic pressures grouped into five major categories: climate (water temperature, air–heat index, sea-level rise), ocean chemistry (ocean acidification and dissolved oxygen), land-based pressures (nutrient inputs, light pollution, and coastal human population density), net primary productivity, and fisheries (biomass removal). Pressure layers are mapped globally at 10-km spatial resolution and combined with habitat-specific vulnerability weights to estimate cumulative impacts on marine habitats [@Halpern2025].

In this study, we used cumulative impact estimates corresponding to present-day conditions (~2010–2020), consistent with the temporal coverage of the food webs analyzed. Impact values represent the average cumulative pressure experienced by marine habitats within each spatial unit, with values $\ge 1$ indicating conditions under which habitats are unlikely to persist in their current state. For each food web, we calculated the mean cumulative human impact index across the spatial extent of the corresponding network and used this value as a continuous predictor in subsequent analyses.

### Estimating variability of metrics using a metaweb model

We assumed that the compiled and standardized food webs represent the full set of potential trophic interactions for each system. Because species may be absent from a given site at particular times, not all potential interactions are necessarily realized, and the local number of species and links may fluctuate through time. To capture this variability, we used a metaweb assembly model [@Saravia2022], treating each compiled food web as the metaweb corresponding to its respective area. Such a modeling framework helps unite local ecological interactions and broader biogeographic patterns and processes [@Mestre2026].

In this model, species colonize a local site from the metaweb with probability $c$ and go locally extinct with probability $e$, following the logic of island biogeography theory [@MacArthur1967] while explicitly incorporating food web structure. Colonizing species arrive with their full set of potential trophic interactions, but only interactions involving species present in the local community are realized. Non-basal species are subject to secondary extinction with probability $se$ when none of their prey are present. Local extinctions may therefore propagate through the network via cascades of secondary extinctions, modulated by $se$.

The three model parameters ($c$, $e$, and $se$) were estimated separately for each compiled food web using approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) [@Beaumont2010]. We used the package `abc` with the rejection algorithm [@Csillery2012]. Model fit was evaluated using the Euclidean distance between observed and simulated values of species richness and connectance. Prior distributions were uniform: $c \sim U(0.01, 0.3)$, $e \sim U(0.001, 0.5)$, and $se \sim U(0.1, 0.9)$. For each web, we ran 10,000 simulations and retained the closest 5% of simulations as accepted parameter sets. The model was implemented in R using the package `meweasmo` [@Saravia2022b].

To assess whether the metaweb assembly model adequately captures the structural properties of compiled food webs, we compared observed network metrics with the distributions obtained from simulated networks. Across all metrics considered--link density, connectance, complexity (SVD), rank deficiency, mean trophic level, and modularity--observed values consistently fell within the range of variation generated by the model (Figures S3–S5), with the exception that link density in compiled networks tended to exceed the simulated distribution, as expected when not all species co-occur simultaneously in simulated networks. This agreement indicates that the metaweb assembly framework reproduces realistic levels of network organization, supporting its use for quantifying variability and uncertainty in food web structure. Unlike the other network metrics considered in this study, dynamic stability already incorporates uncertainty through randomizations of interaction strengths. Therefore, additional variability derived from the metaweb assembly model was not estimated for this metric. For each food web, the site-level mean and standard deviation of every metric across the retained metaweb-derived replicates were used as the point estimate and associated uncertainty in the site-level regression models described below (see Statistical analyses).

### Network metrics

We described the food web complexity, structure and stability using commonly-used and relatively novel metrics in ecological network studies [@Delmas2018; @Landi2018; @Montoya2006]. A definition and the ecological meaning for each metric is provided in Table 1. Details on the methodology to calculate the novel metrics, such as SVD complexity, rank deficiency and dynamic stability, can be found in Supplementary Methods.

#### Statistical analyses

Because our dataset comprises only seven independent food webs, for each food web we summarized the distribution of each network metric across its retained metaweb-derived replicates as a single site-level point estimate (the replicate mean) together with its associated uncertainty (the replicate standard deviation), after applying the transformations described below.

Proportion metrics (C, Modularity, Rank Deficiency) were logit‐transformed, strictly positive variables (Link Density and dynamic stability) were log‐transformed, and SVD complexity and mean trophic level were standardized (z‐scores). Dynamic stability was quantified as $\log(-\lambda_{\max})$, using the eigenvalue with the maximum real part of the community matrix, multiplied by -1 so that larger values indicate a stronger tendency to return to equilibrium.

Each of the seven response metrics was modeled independently as a function of log‐transformed area (km^2^), latitude, mean human impact index, and number of trophic species ($S$), using a Bayesian regression with a measurement-error term (the `se()` function in the `brms` package) that incorporates the site-level standard deviation derived from the metaweb-based replicates directly into the likelihood, together with an additional residual variance component. This yields seven independent site-level observations per model, one per food web, and propagates the uncertainty associated with metaweb-based replication into the estimated relationships. All predictors were centered and scaled prior to analysis, and collinearity among them was assessed with variance inflation factors (VIF), which ranged from 1.68 to 3.10 and did not indicate concerning collinearity (Table S3).

All models were fit with four chains of 4,000 iterations (2,000 warmup) using `brms` with the `CmdStan` backend, and convergence was assessed with R-hat and effective sample size diagnostics. Support for each predictor–response relationship was summarized as the posterior probability of a consistent sign, calculated as the maximum of the posterior probabilities that the slope was positive or negative; we discuss effects for which this probability exceeded 0.90.

Given the small sample size (n = 7), an apparent relationship reaching this threshold under the full dataset can nonetheless be driven by one or two highly influential food webs. We therefore assessed the robustness of every relationship meeting this threshold with a leave-one-site-out procedure: each of the seven models was refit seven times, excluding one food web at a time, and we recorded whether the direction and posterior support ($\geq$ 0.90) of the corresponding effect were preserved. We classify an effect as robust when this was the case in at least four of the seven leave-one-site-out refits (i.e., it failed to hold in no more than three exclusions); effects that failed to hold in four or more refits are reported but interpreted with substantial caution, as they may reflect the influence of one or two food webs rather than a general pattern.

All data transformations, model specifications, priors, and code required to reproduce the analyses, including the site-level restructuring and leave-one-site-out diagnostics described above, are provided in the Supplementary Materials and in a public GitHub repository (https://github.com/EcoComplex/SouthMetawebs), with archived code and data available on Zenodo (doi: xxxxxxxx).

## Results

Across the seven food webs analyzed, network metrics varied markedly in magnitude and variability (Table S1). Connectance (C) and link density (LD) spanned an order of magnitude, with the highest values observed in both Scotia Sea networks and the lowest in Burdwood Bank. Mean trophic level (TL) ranged between 2.2 and 3.5, whereas SVD complexity showed moderate variation among systems. Rank deficiency, reflecting the effective dimensionality of interaction matrices, varied substantially across food webs, with the highest values observed in Burdwood Bank and the Weddell Sea. Modularity also showed a broad range among networks, indicating differing degrees of compartmentalization. Dynamic stability, quantified by the maximum eigenvalue of the community matrix, also differed among systems, with Scotia Sea networks tending to exhibit more negative eigenvalues than lower-latitude food webs, consistent with faster return rates to equilibrium following perturbations.

Site-level Bayesian regressions (n = 7 independent food webs per model; see Methods) identified ecosystem area as the strongest and most consistent predictor of food web structure among the 28 metric–predictor combinations examined, based on posterior support and leave-one-site-out robustness (Figure 2).

![Posterior distributions of standardized slopes for all metric–predictor combinations (seven network metrics by four predictors) from the site-level Bayesian regressions, ordered from the largest positive to the most negative posterior mean. Background shading marks relationships that reached the 0.90 posterior support threshold and remained robust to leave-one-site-out exclusion (blue: positive; salmon: negative); unshaded relationships either did not reach this threshold or did not survive the leave-one-site-out check (Table S2).](Figures/Bayesian_post_slopes.png)

Log-transformed area was positively associated with mean trophic level (posterior probability of a consistent positive sign, p = 0.974), SVD complexity (p = 0.965), connectance (p = 0.956), and link density (p = 0.949) (Figure 3). These four relationships were also the only ones that survived a leave-one-site-out robustness check: each remained above the 0.90 support threshold, with a consistent sign, in at least four of the seven leave-one-site-out refits (Table S2), indicating they are not driven by any single food web.

![Marginal effects of ecosystem area on mean trophic level, SVD complexity, connectance, and link density, in each metric's original units, the four relationships that remained robust to excluding any single food web. Solid black lines represent posterior mean predictions from the site-level Bayesian models, back-transformed to each metric's original scale; shaded areas indicate 95% credible intervals. Colored points show the observed mean for each food web, computed directly from the metaweb-derived replicates, with vertical bars indicating their 95% quantiles.](Figures/Bayesian_TL_SVDC_LD_vs_Area_mv_origscale.png)

Several additional relationships reached the same nominal posterior support threshold ($\geq$ 0.90) under the full dataset but did not survive this check. A negative association between area and modularity (p = 0.931) reversed sign or fell below the support threshold in all seven leave-one-site-out refits and is not interpreted as a genuine pattern, consistent with it being a likely artifact of overfitting in a dataset of only seven food webs. Positive associations between latitude and connectance (p = 0.923), link density (p = 0.908), trophic level (p = 0.900), and SVD complexity (p = 0.939), and associations between the number of trophic species (S) and modularity (p = 0.938), rank deficiency (p = 0.914), and, negatively, connectance (p = 0.925), similarly failed to survive exclusion of at least five of the seven food webs (Table S2), and we treat these as exploratory rather than general findings. Effects of dynamic stability on area, latitude and S did not reach the 0.90 support threshold (p = 0.733, 0.730, and 0.691, respectively).

Effects of human impact were comparatively weak and uncertain, with no predictor–response combination reaching the 0.90 support threshold (maximum p = 0.819, for SVD complexity).

Variance inflation factors for the four predictors ranged from 1.68 (human impact) to 3.10 (number of trophic species), well below conventional thresholds for concerning collinearity (Table S3), indicating that the uncertainty surrounding the latitude- and species-related effects described above is more likely related to the small number of independent food webs than to correlated predictors.

## Discussion

<!-- Párrafo sobre area -->
Ecosystem area emerged as the primary and most robust driver of food web structure and complexity across the studied systems, with larger ecosystems supporting higher trophic levels, greater interaction density, and higher structural complexity (SVD complexity). Unlike every other relationship considered in this study, these associations with area remained above the 0.90 posterior support threshold in at least four of the seven leave-one-site-out refits, indicating they are not an artifact of any single system. Such patterns are consistent with theoretical expectations that larger ecosystems can sustain more complex food webs through greater spatial extent, increased habitat availability, and enhanced persistence of higher trophic levels [@Galiana2018;@Gravel2011; @Takimoto2013]. Food webs from larger ecosystems also exhibited higher interaction density, indicating a greater diversity of trophic pathways and potentially higher trophic redundancy, which may buffer perturbations by providing alternative routes of energy transfer when particular interactions are disrupted [@Biggs2020; @Sanders2018]. Given the robustness of this pattern relative to every other relationship considered here, we regard ecosystem area as the most defensible driver of marine food web organization identified in this study.

<!-- Modularidad: reencuadrado como no robusto -->
An apparent negative association between modularity and ecosystem area, broadly consistent with patterns previously reported in some marine food webs [@Albouy2019; @Montoya2015], was detected under the full dataset (posterior probability of a negative slope = 0.931) but did not survive a leave-one-site-out check: it reversed sign or lost support whenever any single food web was excluded from the analysis. With only seven independent food webs in our compiled dataset, we cannot distinguish a genuine negative relationship between modularity and ecosystem area from an artifact driven by one or two systems with unusual modularity values, most plausibly the Scotia Sea networks, which are predominantly pelagic and lack a clear separation between benthic and pelagic compartments, a habitat segregation that can otherwise promote compartmentalization [@Eskuche-Keith2023]. We therefore do not interpret this relationship further here and flag it as a hypothesis that would require additional independent food webs, ideally spanning a wider range of habitat compositions, to test properly.

<!-- Párrafo sobre el número de especies: reencuadrado como exploratorio -->
Effects of trophic species richness (S) on connectance, rank deficiency, and modularity reached the same nominal posterior support threshold as ecosystem area under the full dataset, but were considerably less robust: each failed the leave-one-site-out check in at least five of the seven exclusions. The previously hypothesized trade-off between species richness and connectance (whereby the number of realized interactions increases more slowly than the number of possible interactions as species accumulate [@Dunne2002; @Vermaat2009]) therefore remains plausible in principle but is not established by the present dataset. Testing it robustly, together with the associated hypotheses regarding rank deficiency and modularity, will require additional independent food webs spanning a broader range of species richness than are currently available for the Southwest Atlantic and Antarctic region.

<!-- Párrafos sobre latitud: reencuadrados como exploratorios -->
Latitude was positively associated with connectance, link density, trophic level and SVD complexity under the full dataset, consistent with previous reports that connectance in marine food webs tends to increase toward higher latitudes [@Albouy2019]. However, none of these associations was robust to excluding individual food webs: each lost posterior support or reversed sign in the majority of leave-one-site-out refits. We regard the latitudinal patterns detected here as exploratory rather than established, pending confirmation with additional independent food webs spanning a broader range of latitudes.

<!-- Párrafos sobre HII: sin cambios sustanciales. Aca relaciona principalmente la modularidad como una respuesta a perturbaciones antropicas, tambien podriamos hablar de dynamic stability (resiliencia) como  esperariamos que responda, con citas-->

Given the widely accepted view that modularity can enhance food web stability by limiting the propagation of perturbations [@Eskuche-Keith2023], we initially expected a positive relationship between modularity and the human impact index. However, no such relationship was detected, either under the full dataset or in the site-level analysis reported here. One possible explanation is that human pressures may simultaneously promote and erode modularity through opposing mechanisms. While disturbance can favor compartmentalization by isolating impacts, chronic anthropogenic stressors often homogenize ecosystems by selectively removing sensitive species and interactions, thereby reducing network compartmentalization. This interpretation is consistent with the findings of @Mestre2022, who showed that fishing pressure can erode modular structure in marine food webs. The combined action of these opposing processes could result in a net neutral relationship between modularity and overall human impact in our analysis. Moreover, the composite nature of the human impact index may mask contrasting effects of its individual components on modularity and other network metrics. Disentangling these component‐specific effects represents an important avenue for future research.

Beyond the limitations of the composite human impact index, another constraint on detecting anthropogenic effects stems from the nature of the food web data themselves. The networks analyzed here capture the topology of trophic interactions (the presence or absence of links between species) but not the frequency, intensity, or proportional contribution of them. Anthropogenic stressors such as fisheries, pollution, or climate change may alter the strength of trophic links or shift diet composition without adding or removing the links themselves. For example, in the San Jorge Gulf, there is evidence that several fish species have shifted their diets over recent decades [@Belleggia2019, @Pasti2024], yet for most species, no updated dietary information has been available since 2000 [@Rincon-Diaz2024]. As long as a trophic interaction persists between species, even if its quantitative importance changes substantially, such reorganization remains invisible in a binary adjacency matrix. In this sense, binary food web topology is relatively insensitive to the kind of gradual reorganization mediated by interaction strength that anthropogenic stressors typically drive. Moreover, the dietary information underlying these networks was compiled from studies spanning several decades, with data for different species collected across different periods, locations, and ecological contexts. This temporal heterogeneity means that the networks represent a time-averaged, composite snapshot of trophic structure rather than a record tied to any specific period, even if the human impact index was computed for present-day conditions (2010–2020). Resolving these limitations would require quantitatively weighted food webs in which interaction strengths and/or diets are restricted to a particular period. The construction of weighted food webs with most interactions restricted to a particular period would be important for future efforts to use food web structure as an indicator of anthropogenic impact in marine ecosystems.

<!-- Modularidad y estabilidad: reducido a un parrafo, ya no es un resultado del estudio -->
Modularity and dynamic stability are often hypothesized to trade off against one another because they capture different dimensions of a food web's response to perturbation: resistance to the spread of disturbance versus the rate of return to equilibrium [@Donohue2016; @Thebault2010; @Carpentier2021]. Our data do not provide robust support for this trade-off in either direction: none of the modularity-related associations with ecosystem area or species richness, nor any of the dynamic-stability-related associations with area, latitude or species richness, survived the leave-one-site-out check reported above. We note the hypothesized trade-off here as motivated by prior theoretical and empirical work rather than as a finding of the present analysis, and see it as a candidate pattern worth revisiting once a larger set of independent food webs becomes available.

<!-- Conclusiones -->
To determine whether the relationships identified here represent general features of marine food webs or patterns specific to the Southwest Atlantic-Antarctic region, additional highly resolved food webs from other marine basins will be needed, a limitation made explicit by the leave-one-site-out diagnostics applied throughout this study, which showed that several apparent relationships did not survive the exclusion of individual food webs. At present, marine food web research remains geographically imbalanced, with a disproportionate focus on Northern Hemisphere ecosystems [@Xu2024; @Poisot2021]. Expanding the availability of comparable food web datasets from the Southern Hemisphere will be essential both for evaluating the generality of the patterns detected here and for supporting more complex multivariate models than the seven independent food webs currently available can reliably identify.

By integrating observed food webs with metaweb-derived uncertainty at the site level and leave-one-site-out validation, we provide a conservative assessment of how environmental gradients shape marine trophic architecture. Ecosystem area, independently of species richness, is the only driver identified here whose association with food web structure, specifically higher trophic levels, greater interaction density, and higher structural complexity, is robust to the exclusion of any single food web. Associations involving latitude, species richness, and modularity, while detected under the full dataset, should be treated as hypotheses for future work with an expanded, more geographically representative set of food webs rather than as established patterns.

More broadly, this study illustrates a practical safeguard for macroecological analyses built on a small number of independent replicate systems: a posterior support threshold alone, however conservative, is not sufficient evidence of a general effect when each observational unit carries substantial leverage. A leave-one-site-out check of this kind, while inherently limited with n = 7 food webs, distinguishes patterns that are more likely to be general from those that are contingent on a small number of systems, and we recommend a similar approach for other macroecological syntheses built on comparably small compiled datasets.
